newsitem.title: USA: Layoffs rose 8.5 percent in 1996 - Challenger.
newsitem.headline: Layoffs rose 8.5 percent in 1996 - Challenger.

text.p: Job cuts in the United States rose in 1996, but are expected to fall 10 percent to 15 percent this year as the economy's strength is prompting companies to think twice about laying off workers, a survey released Wednesday showed.

The new trend has already begun, with layoffs plunging 32 percent to 37,402 in December from 55,237 in the same month in 1995, according to the survey by Challenger, Gray & Christmas Inc., an employment firm that tracks job cuts daily.
However, December's lay-offs were 26.6 percent higher than the 29,537 in November, it said.
For all of 1996, U.S. job cuts rose 8.5 percent 477,147 from 439,882 in 1995.

"The slowdown in job cuts in the second half of 1996 may be a harbinger of things to come," said John Challenger, executive vice president of the outplacement firm. "With the dramatic growth in high-tech fields, other industries are finding it difficult to find top technical performers to hire."
One company offered employees $2,500 for each person they referred that the firm hired, he said.

"In 1997, job cuts could be 10 percent to 15 percent lower than last year because today's economy is strong and a tight labour market has caused companies to rethink their former stance about the disposability of people, especialy in the case of mergers," Challenger said.
Slashing more workers from the payroll would be too risky when some companies are already stretched thin during a period of low unemployment and severe spot labour shortages, he said.
In many industries, experienced rank-and-file employees have become a "protected class" because replacing them can be very difficult, Challenger added.
However, middle managers remain vulnerable to lay-offs because companies cannot afford to be weighed down by the cost of employing them at the risk of losing their skilled workers, he said.

"In 1997, we will probably see more efforts on the part of management to instill a feeling of loyalty and commitment among employees. The economic benefits of employee loyalty often explain why one company is more profitable than another," Challenger said.

Industries that will continue to cut jobs significantly in 1997 will be in newly deregulated sectors such as utilities, finance and telecommunications, he said. Heavy cuts in retailing are possible once Christmas sales figures are in.

Telecommunications led industry sectors with the most announced job cuts in 1996, with 43,702, followed by retailing, with 42,025, computers, with 36,930, food, with 34,453, and autos, with 33,233, Challenger said.
